section1.title: What do you supply?
section1.guidance:
# What's this section for?

We use your selected category to decide which sections of the questionnaire you'll see. This keeps the form short and ensures you're only asked about the products or services you provide.

For example:

* A coffee stall won't be asked about temporary structures.
* A structures contractor won't be asked food-related questions.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

**Yes.** All suppliers start here, and it takes less than a minute to complete.

---

# What to enter

Select your **Primary Category** — the category representing the largest share of what you supply to this event, based on:

* Volume of goods or services provided
* Contract value
* Overall scope of work

If you provide more than one type of product or service, also select a **Secondary Category**.

If you only supply one type of product or service, no secondary category is required.

---

# Examples

* **A caterer who also provides a small marquee**

  * Primary: *Food & Beverage Services*
  * Secondary: *Temporary Structures & Infrastructure*

* **A generator hire company**

  * Primary: *Energy, Power & Utilities*
  * No secondary category

* **A stewarding and security provider**

  * Primary: *Staffing, Workforce & Security*

* **An AV and digital signage provider**

  * Primary: *Broadcast, Media, IT & Connectivity*

---

# Good to know

The sections shown to you are based on the combination of your primary and secondary categories.

If you later realize that something is missing, or your category selection is incorrect, simply update your categories and the questionnaire will adjust automatically.

section2.title: How we'll work out your footprint
section2.guidance:
# How would you like us to calculate the carbon footprint of your supply?

To calculate the carbon footprint of your supply to this event, we first need to understand what information you already have available.

The questionnaire will automatically show only the questions relevant to your selection. For goods suppliers, your choice will also determine which columns appear in the data entry tables.

---

# Option A — I have a carbon footprint report or label for my products

Choose this option if you already have **product-level carbon data** for the goods supplied to this event, such as:

* A Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) report
* An Environmental Product Declaration (EPD)
* Another verified product-specific carbon assessment

If you select this option, the goods sections will include additional fields for:

* Your carbon footprint value
* Units of measure
* The standard, methodology, or source used

### Examples

* A brewery that knows the footprint per litre of its beer.
* A manufacturer with an EPD for a structure or building material.

---

# Option B — I don't have that, please estimate it for me

Choose this option if you supply physical goods but do not have product-level carbon data.

Simply tell us:

* What you supplied
* How much you supplied

We will apply recognised industry emission factors to estimate the footprint.

This is the most commonly selected option and is typical for:

* Food and beverage suppliers
* Merchandise suppliers
* Equipment providers
* Temporary structures and infrastructure suppliers

---

# Option C — I'd rather provide my company's overall operational figures

Choose this option if you primarily provide services, such as:

* Security
* Staffing
* Professional services
* Consultancy

It is also suitable if your company already tracks its annual emissions or energy consumption.

We will calculate only the share of your company's footprint that relates to this event.

If you choose this option, we'll ask for:

* Annual Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions **or** annual energy consumption
* The reporting period used
* An allocation method

**Revenue-based allocation is recommended.**

### Worked example

* Annual revenue: **£2,000,000**
* Event invoice value: **£40,000**
* Event share of revenue: **2%**
* Annual Scope 1 and 2 emissions: **500 tCO₂e**

**Event footprint = 2% × 500 = 10 tCO₂e**

---

# If you choose Option C — the golden rule

Make sure your:

* Energy data
* Carbon emissions data
* Financial or operational allocation data

all relate to the **same 12-month reporting period**.

If your current reporting year is not yet complete, you can:

1. Use your most recently completed reporting year (preferred).
2. Provide a reasonable estimate for the current year.
3. Provide a direct percentage estimate of activity related to this event.

---

# Good to know

An honest estimate with clear assumptions is far more useful than leaving fields blank.

section6.title: Food & Beverage
section6.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures the carbon footprint of the food and drink supplied to this event.

Different foods have very different environmental impacts. For example, beef generally has a much higher carbon footprint than vegetables, so we collect each food item separately.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if you supplied food or beverages to this event.

If not, answer **No** to the gateway question and this section will be skipped automatically.

---

# What to enter

### Food table

Add one row for each food item supplied. For each row:

1. Select the **Food Product Category**.
2. Enter the **Quantity Supplied to This Event**.
3. Choose the appropriate **Unit of Measurement**.

### Beverages table

Use the separate beverages table for drinks, including:

* Beer
* Wine
* Spirits
* Soft drinks
* Tea
* Coffee
* Other beverages

---

# Examples

* **500 beef burgers (approximately 125 g each)**

  * Category: Beef
  * Quantity: 62.5
  * Unit: kg

* **1,200 pints of beer**

  * Category: Beer
  * Quantity: 680
  * Unit: litres
  * *(entered in the beverages table)*

* **1,000 portions of chips**

  * Category: Potatoes
  * Quantity: 1,000 portions
  * *(or enter the weight if known)*

---

# If you're not sure

A reasonable estimate is perfectly acceptable. Please record any assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Important

* Report quantities for **this event only**, not annual totals.
* If you already have Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) or Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) data, return to **"How we'll work out your footprint"** and select **Option A**. The tables in this section will automatically switch to the PCF version.

section7.title: Temporary Structures & Event Infrastructure
section7.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures the carbon footprint of temporary structures and event infrastructure supplied or installed for this event.

Examples include:

* Marquees
* Staging
* Grandstands
* Fencing
* Crowd barriers
* Temporary stands and other infrastructure

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if you supplied or installed temporary structures for this event.

If not, answer **No** to the gateway question and this section will be skipped automatically.

---

# What to enter

Add one row for each structure supplied.

For each row, provide:

1. **Structure Type**
2. **Ownership / Hire Status** (Owned or Hired)
3. **Primary Material** (steel, aluminium, timber, fabric, etc.)
4. **Total Weight or Area**
5. **Unit of Measurement**

   * Use **kg** or **tonnes** if the weight is known.
   * Use **m²** if the weight is unknown.
6. **Expected Lifespan (Uses)**

   * Estimate how many events the structure is expected to serve during its lifetime.
7. **Recycled Content (%)**

   * Enter this if known, otherwise leave blank.

---

# Examples

### Hired steel marquee

* Structure Type: Marquee
* Ownership Status: Hired
* Primary Material: Steel
* Area: 200 m²
* Expected Lifespan: 40 uses

*(Example: a 10 m × 20 m marquee with unknown weight.)*

### Hired aluminium grandstand

* Structure Type: Grandstand
* Ownership Status: Hired
* Primary Material: Aluminium
* Weight: 12 tonnes
* Expected Lifespan: 50 uses

### Reusable timber staging

* Structure Type: Staging
* Ownership Status: Owned
* Primary Material: Timber
* Weight: 800 kg
* Expected Lifespan: 30 uses

---

# If you're not sure

A reasonable estimate of the structure's weight or area is perfectly acceptable.

Please record any assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Important

**Reuse significantly reduces the footprint of temporary structures.**

The expected lifespan spreads the manufacturing impact across all uses. For example, a marquee used at 40 events carries only a small fraction of its manufacturing footprint at each event.

section9.title: Deliveries to the event
section9.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures the transport emissions associated with delivering your goods to the event.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if **you arranged and paid for the transport yourself**.

If transport was arranged by:

* A Silverstone contractor, or
* A courier or logistics provider you did not arrange,

answer **No** and skip this section. Those emissions are captured elsewhere.

We'll also ask whether the vehicles used were:

* **Company-owned**, or
* **Hired**

as this affects how emissions are calculated.

---

# How this section works

Transport is divided into four separate tables:

* **Road**
* **Rail**
* **Sea**
* **Air**

Complete only the table(s) that match how your goods travelled and leave the others blank.

Most suppliers only need to complete **Deliveries by Road**.

Add one row for each delivery route.

---

# What to enter — Road transport

For each delivery, enter:

* Vehicle type
* Fuel type
* One-way distance (km)
* Number of trips
* Weight carried

### Optional information

You may also enter:

* **Actual fuel used (litres)** — this is the most accurate method and takes priority over distance-based estimates.
* **Did the vehicle return empty?**
* **Vehicle load factor / how full the vehicle was**

If you're unsure, leave the optional fields at their default values.

---

# What to enter — Rail, Sea and Air transport

For each route, enter:

* One-way distance
* Weight carried
* Unit of measurement
* Number of trips

---

# Examples

### Road delivery

A diesel van delivering stock from 80 km away over three trips:

* Vehicle: Van
* Fuel: Diesel
* One-way distance: 80 km
* Trips: 3
* Weight: Enter the weight carried

### Actual fuel data available

If the van consumed **60 litres of diesel in total**, enter the fuel quantity and we will use that directly instead of estimating from distance.

### Rail delivery

A pallet weighing 0.4 tonnes arriving by rail from 200 km away:

* Distance: 200 km
* Weight: 0.4 tonnes
* Trips: 1

---

# If you're not sure of the distance

Estimate the distance from the origin location using a map or route planner.

Please record any assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Important

Enter **one-way distances only**.

The return journey will be added automatically during the calculation.

section10.title: Your team's travel and overnight stays
section10.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures travel associated with your team's work on this event, including:

* Daily travel to and from the event site
* Long-distance journeys made specifically for the event
* Overnight stays away from home

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if any staff:

* Travelled to the event site on a daily basis,
* Made long-distance journeys specifically for the event, or
* Stayed overnight away from home.

If none of these apply, answer **No** and the travel sections will be skipped automatically.

---

# What to enter

### Daily staff travel

Choose one of the following options:

* **Aggregated (recommended)** — provide one set of totals for the whole team.
* **Individual** — enter one row per person.
* **No daily staff travel** — if nobody travelled to and from the site each day.

### Overnight stays

Answer **Yes** if any staff stayed away from home for the event.

### Long-distance travel

Answer **Yes** if any staff made a dedicated long-distance journey for the event, such as:

* Flights
* Long train journeys
* Long-distance car travel

---

# Example

A local crew of **8 staff working over 3 days**, with:

* **2 staff staying overnight**, and
* **1 staff member flying in from abroad**

would select:

* **Aggregated daily travel**
* **Yes** to overnight stays
* **Yes** to long-distance travel

---

# Important

Overnight stays are recorded separately.

Any days spent away from home are automatically excluded from daily commuting calculations, ensuring the same travel is not counted twice.

section12.title: Long-Distance Business Travel
section12.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures longer journeys made specifically for this event, separate from day-to-day commuting.

Examples include:

* Flights
* Long-distance train journeys
* Long-distance car travel
* Other dedicated journeys made to reach the venue

In carbon reporting terms, these journeys are considered **business travel** for the event (GHG Protocol Scope 3, Category 6).

Unlike the **Daily Staff Travel** section, which captures routine travel to and from the event site, this section covers one-off journeys made for a specific engagement.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if you answered **Yes** to **Long-Distance Travel** in the travel overview section.

If not, this section will be skipped automatically.

---

# What to enter

Add one row for each type of journey.

For each row, enter:

* **Travel Type**

  * Select the closest option available.
  * For flights, choose the option that matches the cabin class where applicable.
* **Number of staff** who made the journey
* **Distance unit** (km or miles)
* **One-way distance**
* **Number of return trips made by each person**

---

# Examples

### National rail travel

Four staff travelling by rail:

* Travel Type: National Rail
* Number of staff: 4
* Distance: 150 km (one way)
* Return trips per person: 1

### International flight

Two staff travelling internationally in economy class:

* Travel Type: International Flight (Economy)
* Number of staff: 2
* Distance: 1,200 km (one way)
* Return trips per person: 1

---

# Important

* Enter **one-way distances only**.
* Record each distinct journey type separately.

Flight emissions include the additional warming effects associated with emissions released at altitude (**radiative forcing**).

As a result, flight emissions are higher than distance alone might suggest. This is standard practice and is already included in the calculation.

section13.title: Overnight stays
section13.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures the carbon footprint of overnight accommodation used by your team for this event.

Where staff stayed matters, as the footprint of accommodation can vary significantly between countries and accommodation types.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if any staff stayed overnight away from home for this event.

If nobody stayed overnight, this section does not apply.

---

# What to enter

Add one row for each country or accommodation type used.

For each row, enter:

* **Country**
* **Accommodation Type** (hotel, B&B, hostel, campsite, etc.)
* **Total Room-Nights**
* **Number of Staff Staying**

### Calculating room-nights

Room-nights are based on the number of rooms used, not the number of people.

**Room-nights = Number of rooms × Number of nights**

---

# Examples

### Shared accommodation

Four staff sharing two twin rooms for three nights:

* Rooms: 2
* Nights: 3
* Room-nights: **6**
* Staff staying: **4**

### Single occupancy

One person staying in their own room for two nights:

* Room-nights: **2**
* Staff staying: **1**

---

# If you're not sure

A reasonable estimate of room-nights is perfectly acceptable.

Please record any assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Important

These are the same overnight stays identified in the **Daily Staff Travel** section.

Accommodation is recorded here, and the corresponding days are automatically excluded from commuting calculations to ensure the same activity is never counted twice.

section14.title: Water

What's this section for?
Water used as part of your activity at the event, and the wastewater generated with it.
Do I need to fill this in?

What to enter
One row per supply: the Water Supply Type; the Volume Supplied in m³; and the Wastewater Generated in m³. 1 m³ = 1,000 litres, so 2,000 litres is 2 m³. If wastewater wasn't measured, assuming it roughly equals the water used is acceptable. If you provided portable toilets, describe them in the Portable Toilets field - how many, and how often serviced.
Examples
2,000 litres brought in for catering and hand-washing → supply type; 2; 2.
4 portable toilets serviced twice over the event → describe in the Portable Toilets field with your best estimate of water used.
If you're not sure
A reasonable estimate is fine - note your assumption, and mention any water reuse or reduction measures you operate.
Important
Don't include water supplied and paid for by Silverstone - it's already in the venue's footprint.

section16.title: Waste
section16.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures waste generated by your activities during the:

* Build period
* Live event
* Breakdown period

Different waste treatment methods have different environmental impacts, so waste is recorded separately according to how it was managed.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if **you arranged and paid for your own waste collection and disposal**.

If Silverstone's site contractor managed your waste, select:

**"No, Silverstone handled it"**

and skip this section, as those impacts are already included in the venue's footprint.

---

# How this section works

There is a separate table for each disposal method.

Complete only the table(s) that reflect how your waste was actually treated and leave the others blank.

For each table, add one row per waste type and enter:

* Waste type
* Quantity
* Unit of measurement (**kg** or **tonnes**)

---

# What the disposal methods mean

### Recycled into a different product (Open-loop recycling)

Material is recycled into a different type of product.

**Examples:**

* Plastic bottles turned into fleece clothing
* Mixed plastics recycled into construction products

If you're unsure which type of recycling applied, select this option.

### Recycled into the same product (Closed-loop recycling)

Material is recycled back into the same type of product.

**Examples:**

* Glass bottles recycled into new glass bottles
* Aluminium cans recycled into new cans

### Burned to make energy (Incineration with energy recovery)

Waste is sent to a waste-to-energy facility that generates heat or electricity.

### Composted

Organic waste is processed into compost.

Typical examples include:

* Food waste
* Garden waste

### Sent to landfill

Waste is disposed of at a landfill site.

Use this option for:

* General mixed waste
* Unsorted rubbish

### Anaerobic digestion

Separated food waste is broken down without oxygen to produce biogas and other by-products.

---

# Examples

### General waste sent to landfill

* Table: Landfill
* Waste type: General / Mixed Waste
* Quantity: 200
* Unit: kg

### Cardboard recycled

* Table: Open-loop Recycling
* Waste type: Paper & Card
* Quantity: 50
* Unit: kg

### Food waste composted

* Table: Composting
* Waste type: Food Waste
* Quantity: 30
* Unit: kg

---

# If you're not sure

### Unknown disposal method

If you do not know how some waste was treated, record it as **Landfill**. This is the most conservative approach.

### Unknown weight

If you do not know the weight, a standard bin sack typically contains approximately **8-10 kg** of general waste.

Estimate the quantity based on the number of sacks used and record your assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Important

Check the unit carefully before submitting.

**500 kg entered as 500 tonnes creates a thousand-fold error.**

section17.title: General Equipment & Materials
section17.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures the carbon footprint of durable equipment and materials supplied or brought to the event.

This includes items such as:

* Tools and equipment
* Furniture
* AV and production equipment
* Signage
* Barriers
* Other durable goods

This section does **not** include:

* Food and beverages
* Temporary structures
* Vehicles

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if you supplied or brought equipment or durable goods to this event.

If not, answer **No** to the gateway question and this section will be skipped automatically.

---

# What to enter

Add one row for each type of item supplied.

For each row, enter:

* **Equipment / Material Type**
* **Purchased or Rented Status**
* **Total Weight**
* **Quantity / Number of Units**

If you supplied equipment that you already own and regularly reuse, select the option that best reflects **reuse or hire**, rather than treating it as a new purchase.

---

# Examples

### Hired furniture

Fifty hired trestle tables:

* Equipment Type: Furniture (Timber)
* Status: Rented
* Weight: Enter total weight if known
* Quantity: 50 units

### Printed banner

One printed PVC banner measuring approximately 20 m²:

* Equipment Type: Signage (PVC)
* Status: Purchased
* Weight: Approximately 10 kg
* Quantity: 1 unit

### Portable toilets supplied

Two portable toilets supplied for the event:

* Record the units in this section as equipment.
* Any water used for servicing them should be recorded separately in the **Water** section.

---

# If you're not sure

A reasonable estimate of the total weight is perfectly acceptable.

Please record any assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Important

Whether an item is **newly purchased**, **rented**, or **reused** has a significant effect on its footprint.

Rented and reusable equipment generally carries a much lower impact than purchasing new items specifically for the event, so please select the most appropriate option.

section18.title: Energy used on site
section18.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures the fuel and electricity used by your own equipment at the event, including:

* Generators
* Lighting
* Machinery
* Refrigeration equipment
* Other powered equipment

It also captures any refrigerant gas that was topped up or leaked from refrigeration or air-conditioning equipment.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if your equipment used fuel or electricity at the event site.

First, tell us where the energy came from.

### I used the venue's supply

Leave the tables empty.

Silverstone already includes this energy within the venue footprint.

### I brought my own supply

Choose this option if:

* You supplied your own generator, fuel or electricity.
* You used both venue power and your own equipment, but can clearly identify your own consumption using:

  * Fuel receipts
  * Meter or sub-meter readings
  * Cylinder counts
  * Other records

Enter **only your own share**.

### A mix of both

Choose this option only when you genuinely cannot separate your own energy use from the venue's supply.

Enter the total amount used and the footprint will be allocated equally:

* 50% to your footprint
* 50% to Silverstone's footprint

---

# Can you split it?

### Yes — choose "I brought my own"

Examples:

* Your fridges ran on venue power, but you know exactly how much diesel your generator used from fuel receipts.
* You have meter readings for your own temporary power supply.

Enter only the energy you supplied yourself. Venue energy is excluded automatically.

### No — choose "A mix of both"

Examples:

* Equipment ran from a shared distribution board supplied by both venue power and a generator, with no sub-metering.
* You switched between venue power and your own generator during the event but kept no records of when each source was used.

In these cases, enter the total amount known and the footprint will be shared equally.

---

# What to enter

Add one row for each energy source used.

For each row, enter:

* **Fuel Type**
* **Amount Used**
* **Unit of Measurement**

Electricity is included in the fuel list. Select **Electricity** if you used your own electrical supply.

### Typical units

| Energy Source | Typical Unit |
| ------------- | ------------ |
| Diesel        | Litres       |
| Petrol        | Litres       |
| Gas Oil       | Litres       |
| HVO           | Litres       |
| Electricity   | kWh          |
| Natural Gas   | kWh          |
| LPG           | kg           |

### Refrigerants

Only complete the refrigerants table if refrigeration or air-conditioning equipment:

* Required a gas top-up, or
* Experienced a known leak.

---

# Examples

### Diesel generator

A generator consuming 200 litres of diesel:

* Fuel Type: Diesel (100% Mineral)
* Amount Used: 200
* Unit: Litres

### Own electricity supply

A temporary connection using 500 kWh:

* Fuel Type: Electricity
* Amount Used: 500
* Unit: kWh

### Refrigerant top-up

An air-conditioning unit topped up with 0.5 kg of R410A:

* Refrigerant Type: R410A
* Quantity: 0.5 kg

---

# If you're not sure

If you do not know the exact amount used, enter the amount spent and we will estimate the consumption.

Please record any assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Important

* Never enter energy supplied solely by the venue — it is already included in Silverstone's footprint.
* Under **"I brought my own supply"**, enter only your own consumption.
* Under **"A mix of both"**, enter the total amount known and the footprint will be split equally between your organisation and Silverstone.

section19.title: Temporary Structures & Event Infrastructure PCF
section19.guidance:
# What's this section for?

You selected **Option A**, which means you already have Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) or Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) data for some or all of the temporary structures supplied to this event.

In this section, you can provide your own carbon footprint values and we will use those figures wherever they are available.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if you supplied temporary structures or event infrastructure for this event and selected **Option A**.

---

# What to enter

Enter the same information required in the standard structures section, including:

* Structure type
* Ownership or hire status
* Primary material
* Total weight or area
* Unit of measurement
* Expected lifespan (number of uses)
* Recycled content (%), if known

Where available, also provide:

* **PCF / EPD Value**
* **PCF Standard or Source**

Structures and construction products commonly use Environmental Product Declarations published to **EN 15804**.

If you leave the PCF field blank for a structure, we will estimate its footprint using the material and quantity information provided.

---

# Example

### Aluminium grandstand with an EN 15804 EPD

* Enter the structure details as usual.
* PCF / EPD Value: **9.8**
* Source: **EN 15804 EPD**

---

# Important

Make sure the basis of the PCF or EPD matches the quantity you enter.

EPDs may be declared:

* Per kilogram (kg)
* Per square metre (m²)
* Per declared unit

The quantity entered in the table must use the same basis.

We still ask for the **expected lifespan**, because the manufacturing footprint is distributed across all uses of the structure, regardless of where the carbon footprint value originates.

section20.title: Daily staff travel — Aggregated totals
section20.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This section captures the day-to-day travel of your team to and from the event site using a single set of totals for the whole team.

This is the recommended approach for most suppliers.

---

# What to enter

### Total staff deployed (Headcount)

Enter the total number of people who worked at the event.

### Total working days (Person-days)

Add together the number of days worked by all staff.

**Example:**

* 8 staff × 3 days = **24 person-days**

### Overnight person-days

Enter the number of days where staff stayed overnight instead of travelling home.

These days are automatically removed from commuting calculations so they are not double-counted with accommodation.

**Example:**

* 2 staff staying for 3 nights = **6 overnight person-days**

### Distance unit and average one-way commute distance

Enter the typical home-to-site distance for **one person**, one way.

Use either:

* Kilometres (km), or
* Miles

Do not enter the total distance travelled by the whole team.

### Primary transport mode

Select the transport mode used by most of the team and enter the percentage of staff using it.

### Vehicle occupancy

If the primary mode is **car**, enter the average number of people sharing each vehicle.

Examples:

* **1** = everyone drove separately.
* **2** = staff typically travelled in pairs.

This field is only used when the selected transport mode is car.

### Secondary transport mode

If part of the team travelled differently, select the secondary mode and enter the percentage of staff using it.

---

# Worked example

A team of **8 staff** worked **3 days each**.

* 2 staff stayed overnight for all 3 days.
* The average commute distance was 30 km one way.
* 70% of staff travelled by shared car (2 people per vehicle).
* The remaining 30% travelled by train.

The entries would be:

* Headcount: **8**
* Person-days: **24**
* Overnight person-days: **6**
* Distance unit: **km**
* Average one-way distance: **30**
* Primary mode: **Car**
* Vehicle occupancy: **2**
* Primary mode share: **70%**
* Secondary mode: **Train**

The calculation then uses:

* **24 − 6 = 18 commuting person-days**
* 70% allocated to car travel
* 30% allocated to rail travel

---

# If you're not sure

Reasonable averages are perfectly acceptable.

Please record any assumptions in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Good to know

If your team consists of groups with very different travel patterns, enter separate rows for each group rather than using one blended average.

For example:

* A local crew travelling 10 km each day
* A touring crew travelling 150 km each day

Also remember that long journeys made specifically to attend the event should be recorded in the **Long-Distance Business Travel** section.

This section is intended only for routine daily commuting.

---

# Important

Enter the distance for **one person, one way**.

The return journey is added automatically, and the person-days figure scales the calculation to the whole team.

section22.title: Quality & Data Confidence
section22.guidance:
# What's this section for?

This final section provides a short and honest summary of the quality and completeness of your data.

It helps us:

* Understand which figures are based on measured data and which are estimates.
* Calculate data quality scores.
* Record assumptions and known gaps.
* Make your submission more transparent and audit-ready.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

**Yes.**

All suppliers complete this section, and it usually takes only a few minutes.

---

# What to enter

### Primary data sources

Add one row for each type of information source used to complete the questionnaire.

Examples include:

* Invoices and meter readings
* Supplier records
* Internal business records
* Estimates
* Industry averages

For each source, provide the approximate percentage of your answers that came from that source.

The percentages should add up to approximately **100%**.

### Data completeness (%)

Estimate how much of your event activity is covered by the information provided.

Examples:

* **95-100%** = almost all activity captured
* **80%** = some information missing
* **Below 80%** = significant gaps or heavy reliance on estimates

### Known exclusions or data gaps

Record anything you could not include.

Examples:

* Waste weights for Day 1 not recorded
* Fuel use for one hired generator unavailable
* Missing delivery information from a subcontractor

### Assumptions and estimates

Describe any assumptions used to complete the questionnaire.

Examples:

* Average commute distance estimated at 30 km from staff postcodes
* General waste estimated using the number of bin bags generated
* Hotel room-nights estimated from booking records

---

# Example

### Primary data sources

* Invoices and meter readings — 60%
* Estimates — 40%

### Data completeness

* 90%

### Known exclusions

* Fuel consumption for one hired generator was unavailable.

### Assumptions

* General waste estimated using 9 kg per bin bag.

---

# Good to know

An honest estimate with a clear explanation is far more valuable than an unsupported guess.

You will not be penalised for using estimates. In most cases, clearly documented assumptions are preferable to leaving fields blank.

Submitting the questionnaire confirms that the information provided is accurate to the best of your knowledge.

section23.title: Food & Beverage PCF
section23.guidance:
# What's this section for?

You selected **Option A**, which means you already have Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) data for the food and drink supplied to this event.

In this section, you provide your own product carbon footprint values and we use these figures instead of standard industry emission factors.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if you supplied food or beverages to this event.

If you did not supply food or drink, this section does not apply.

---

# What to enter

Use the **Food Product Data** table for food items and the **Beverage Product Data** table for drinks.

Add one row for each product supplied and enter:

1. The product category.
2. The quantity supplied to this event.
3. Your **PCF Value**.
4. The **PCF Standard or Source** used.

Acceptable sources include:

* Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs)
* ISO 14067
* PAS 2050
* GHG Protocol Product Standard
* Other recognised product carbon assessments

### Unit consistency

Enter the PCF value using the unit shown in the table (**kgCO₂e per kg**) and make sure the quantity uses the same basis.

For example:

* A PCF expressed per kilogram requires the quantity to be entered in kilograms.
* If your PCF is reported per litre or per item, convert it where possible or explain the basis in the final **Assumptions and Estimates** section.

---

# Examples

* **Bottled beer with a verified PCF of 0.55 kgCO₂e per kg**

  * Category: Beer
  * Quantity: Entered in kg
  * PCF Value: 0.55
  * Source: EPD

* **Bread with a PAS 2050 assessment of 1.1 kgCO₂e per kg**

  * Category: Bread
  * Quantity: Entered in kg
  * PCF Value: 1.1
  * Source: PAS 2050

---

# If some products don't have PCF data

Enter the products for which you have PCF information.

For any products without PCF data, record them under **Known Exclusions or Data Gaps** in the final section so they can be estimated separately.

---

# Important

Quantities and PCF values must use the same basis.

**Mismatched units are the most common error in product-level carbon data.**

section24.title: General Equipment & Materials PCF
section24.guidance:
# What's this section for?

You selected **Option A**, which means you already have Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) or Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) data for some or all of the equipment and materials supplied to this event.

In this section, you can provide your own carbon footprint values and we will use those figures wherever they are available.

---

# Do I need to fill this in?

Only if you supplied equipment or durable materials for this event and selected **Option A**.

---

# What to enter

Enter the same information required in the standard equipment section, including:

* Equipment or material type
* Purchased, rented, or reused status
* Total weight
* Quantity or number of units

Where available, also provide:

* **PCF / EPD Value**
* **PCF Standard or Source**

Acceptable sources include:

* Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs)
* ISO 14067
* PAS 2050
* GHG Protocol Product Standard
* Other recognised product carbon assessments

If you leave the PCF field blank for an item, we will estimate its footprint using recognised industry emission factors.

---

# Example

### Modular aluminium staging with an EPD

* Enter the equipment details as usual.
* PCF / EPD Value: **8.2**
* Source: **EPD**

---

# Important

Make sure the basis of the PCF matches the quantity entered.

For example:

* Use **per kilogram (kg)** values when quantities are entered by weight.
* Use **per unit** values when quantities are entered as item counts.

Including the standard or source used helps ensure the data is transparent, traceable, and auditable.

question1781153727967.title: What equipment or materials did you bring or supply?
question1781153727967.helpText:
Tell us about any durable equipment or goods you brought or supplied for this event — anything that is **not food, a temporary structure, or a vehicle**.

We only need this section if you supplied equipment for the event. We'll ask whether the items were **purchased specifically for the event** or **hired/reused**, as these have different carbon impacts.

Please include only the equipment used for this event, not your full inventory.

A best estimate is fine if exact information is not available.
